title: The One Where Joey Moves Out

jokes.text: Ever realize Cap'n Crunch's eyebrows are on his hat? / That's what's weird? The man's been captain of a cereal for 40 years.
jokes.setup: Joey notices the quirky detail that Cap'n Crunch's eyebrows are on his hat, expecting that to be the surprising observation.
jokes.punchline: Chandler reframes the whole scenario — the truly weird thing is that a man has been commanding a cereal for four decades, not his eyebrow placement.
jokes.explanation: A strong cold open. The misdirection is elegant — the audience expects a reaction to the eyebrow observation, but Chandler zooms out to the more absurd macro level. Sharp two-step structure, good economy, and fits both characters well. Not quite at the 8-anchor level but genuinely clever.

dialogue.line: Character makes random cereal observation. Absurd detail about cartoon mascot anatomy

jokes.text: The spoon! You licked and you put.
jokes.setup: Joey does something with a shared spoon that grosses Chandler out.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's horrified coinage of 'you licked and you put' — an improvised but perfectly descriptive phrase for double-dipping with saliva.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'you licked and you put' is a miniature comic invention — broken syntax that perfectly conveys disgust. It's economical and character-appropriate for an exasperated Chandler. Functional and memorable without being exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I've been the Captain of a cereal box for thirty years. I think I'm allowed to have one weird eyebrow.

jokes.text: You used my toothbrush? / Only because I used the red one to unclog the drain. / Mine is the red one!
jokes.setup: Chandler confronts Joey about sharing a toothbrush; Joey defends himself by revealing he'd already used the 'other' toothbrush for something far worse.
jokes.punchline: The red toothbrush he used to unclog the drain is Chandler's — a horror compounded on top of horror.
jokes.explanation: Classic escalation structure — we think the grossness peaks at double-dipping, then Joey reveals the toothbrush used for drain unclogging is Chandler's. The turn is well-timed and the audience reaction would be visceral. Solid construction.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more disgusting? You just licked that and you put it back!

jokes.text: Oh, God! Can open. Worms everywhere!
jokes.setup: Joey realizes he has now accidentally revealed a chain of disgusting misdeeds (drain toothbrush = Chandler's toothbrush) and tries to process what he's done.
jokes.punchline: Joey's folksy idiom delivered with resigned self-awareness: 'Can open. Worms everywhere.' A malaprop-adjacent, compressed version of 'opened a can of worms.'
jokes.explanation: This is peak Joey voice. The fragmented syntax — stripping the idiom down to its bare nouns — is perfectly Joey. He understands the metaphor well enough to deploy it but delivers it with the bluntness of someone who skipped the verb. High quotability, exceptional economy and character integration. The best of the cold open sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I used your toothbrush. But in my defense, I thought it was mine.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How could you think that was yours? It was in my bathroom!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, I know. Look, I'm sorry. But hey, at least I didn't use it to scrub the toilet like I did last week.

jokes.text: The next time you shower, think about the last thing I wash and the first thing you wash.
jokes.setup: Joey argues soap is self-cleaning so sharing it is fine. Chandler needs a final, devastating counter-argument.
jokes.punchline: Chandler invites Joey to mentally trace the route of a shared bar of soap — the implied body parts make the grossness self-evident and impossible to un-think.
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in implication over exposition. Chandler never says the words — he just sets up the mental exercise and lets the audience's imagination do the work. The structure is tight, the economy is excellent (no wasted syllables), and the unsaid punchline lands harder than any explicit version would. One of the episode's better crafted jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You used my toothbrush?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, mine fell in the drain.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! Joey, that's—wait, what do you mean it fell in the drain?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I was cleaning it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: With what?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The toilet brush.

jokes.text: That's lucky. What if her name was Big Ugly Splotch?
jokes.setup: Rachel explains she's getting a lily tattoo because her mom's name is Lily — isn't that sweet?
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately pivots to the nightmare alternative: what if the mom's name had been 'Big Ugly Splotch'?
jokes.explanation: Phoebe at her best — the joke is pure Phoebe logic, going somewhere no sane person would go, but the specific name 'Big Ugly Splotch' is the right level of absurd. It's not just 'what if her name was something ugly' — it's a whole grotesque tattoo-specific image. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, you see, with soap, you wash your whole body. With a toothbrush, it's just your teeth. So if we share soap, we're basically washing each other, which is cool. But a toothbrush? That's just gross, man.

jokes.text: Where you getting it? / On my shoulder. / What? / What's on your shoulder? / A chip. / A tattoo.
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks where Rachel is getting the tattoo; Rachel says 'on my shoulder.'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe takes it literally — 'what's on your shoulder?' — setting up either 'a chip' (idiom) or 'a tattoo' (literal). Rachel delivers both in quick succession.
jokes.explanation: A quick wordplay moment that works as a beat but isn't particularly inventive. The 'chip on your shoulder' redirect is a competent gag but fairly expected. Functions to keep the scene light.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, maybe if you used the soap in the right order, you wouldn't have this problem.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The right order? It's soap, Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Exactly. You start at the top and work your way down.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, are you really giving Joey instructions on how to shower?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Someone has to.

jokes.text: What if it doesn't come out right? It's like having a bad haircut all the time.
jokes.setup: Ross is skeptical about tattoos and is listing his objections.
jokes.punchline: His analogy — a bad tattoo is like a permanent bad haircut — is both accurate and perfectly Ross: sensible, cautious, slightly killjoy.
jokes.explanation: Functional observational joke that also serves as character establishment for Ross's anxious, cautious nature. The analogy is apt but not especially surprising. Gets a mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, you guys look really... fancy. What's the word? Oh yeah - palindrome!

jokes.text: Yeah, for my dad's birthday, I decided to give him a stroke.
jokes.setup: Ross asks if today is the day Monica will tell her parents about her relationship with Richard.
jokes.punchline: Monica's deadpan response — 'I decided to give him a stroke' — uses the birthday context to weaponize dark humor about the parental shock factor.
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-structured dark joke. The economy is excellent — 'I decided to give him a stroke' packs the entire comedic argument into one clause. Good setup-punchline structure embedded in dialogue. Monica's dry delivery makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A guy in a coma is hosting brunch?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, he's been in that coma for three weeks. I think he's had enough time to prepare.

jokes.text: Remember when you were 9 and Richard was 30, Dad said: 'God, I hope they get together.'
jokes.setup: Monica insists her parents wouldn't mind her relationship with Richard.
jokes.punchline: Ross sarcastically imagines their dad, when Monica was 9 and Richard was 30, hopefully predicting they'd end up together — the absurdity of the age gap made concrete.
jokes.explanation: Sharp ironic joke that crystallizes the age-gap absurdity into a very specific, uncomfortable image. Ross voicing Dad's imagined sentiment is structurally elegant. Works well as dark sibling ribbing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Getting a lily tattoo because my mom's name is Lily. What if my mom's name was Bertha? Would I get a Bertha tattoo? That's not a flower, that's a name for a heavy machinery part.

jokes.text: You could come in straddling him, they still wouldn't believe it.
jokes.setup: Monica tries to arrange the group so they don't look like they're covering something up about her and Richard.
jokes.punchline: Ross points out the cover-up attempt is so futile that even an extremely obvious display wouldn't convince their parents of anything.
jokes.explanation: A solid dig at the parents' obliviousness, with a slightly edgy image ('straddling him') that gives it a little extra punch. Competent joke that serves the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What's on your shoulder?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A chip.

jokes.text: Actually, Mom, I think Monica thanked him for the both of us.
jokes.setup: The mother asks if the kids thanked Dr. Burke for the ride.
jokes.punchline: Ross implies Monica 'thanked' Richard in a way beyond ordinary gratitude — a knowing wink delivered as innocent sibling commentary.
jokes.explanation: Ross getting in a subtle dig that only the audience (and Monica) fully understands. Double meaning works well here. Functional and appropriately cheeky without being too broad.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A tattoo is like a permanent bad haircut. You're stuck with it forever, and everyone can see your poor judgment.

jokes.text: Finger cramp! Oh, God! Sorry. Here, let me get that, Mom.
jokes.setup: Monica's mother mentions that Richard 'has some 20-year-old twinkie in the city' — not knowing Monica IS the twinkie. Monica reacts physically.
jokes.punchline: Monica has a visible physical reaction (a 'finger cramp') — a telltale involuntary response to hearing herself described this way, then awkwardly overcorrects.
jokes.explanation: A nice physical beat in the cringe tradition — Monica's body betraying her secret. The 'finger cramp' excuse is suitably flimsy. Works as visual comedy in the multi-cam format.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, I'm sure Dad will be thrilled. 'Hey Dad, I've been sleeping with a man older than you!' What could go wrong?

jokes.text: So Richard's shopping in the junior section?
jokes.setup: The parents are gossiping about Richard's young girlfriend.
jokes.punchline: Jack's euphemism for dating a much younger woman — 'shopping in the junior section' — is a casually delivered, slightly lewd observation from an older man who finds it amusing rather than scandalous.
jokes.explanation: A well-turned phrase. 'Shopping in the junior section' is compact and evocative. Jack's delivery as a mildly envious older man gives it character. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Don't worry, Mon. I'm sure Mom and Dad will be fine with the age difference. After all, they've always said they just want you to be happy... even if it means dating someone who was in high school when you were in college.

jokes.text: She's probably not even pretty. Just young enough so that everything is still pointing up.
jokes.setup: Judy is dismissing the young woman Richard is supposedly seeing.
jokes.punchline: The backhanded qualifier — 'just young enough so that everything is still pointing up' — is a strikingly frank, slightly self-deprecating observation about aging and gravity.
jokes.explanation: A sharper-than-expected line from Judy. The joke subverts its own premise — she's trying to dismiss the girl but ends up making a more honest, unflattering point about what youth actually offers. The image is vivid and the delivery implies Judy knows exactly what she's talking about. Strong for a supporting character.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We can't just hide in here. Mom and Dad will think we're hiding something.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, they're not going to notice. They once didn't realize I had a broken arm for three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's because you didn't tell them.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I wore a cast! A cast, Monica! They thought it was a really commitment-heavy watch.

jokes.text: In the bathroom there's mirrors on both sides of you. When you're in there, it's like peeing with the Rockettes.
jokes.setup: Joey and Chandler are marveling at a great apartment with an impressive bathroom.
jokes.punchline: Joey's description of the mirrored bathroom creates an infinite-reflection visual, which his brain processes as 'like peeing with the Rockettes.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The logic is pure Joey: mirrors create infinite reflections of yourself → your brain sees a row of identical figures → the Rockettes are a row of identical figures doing the same thing → therefore, mirrored-bathroom peeing = Rockettes. The leap is absurd but internally consistent, and only Joey would arrive at this comparison with complete sincerity. Highly quotable, visually memorable, and perfectly character-integrated. Approaches the 8-anchor calibration.

jokes.text: Well, there's my fantasy come true.
jokes.setup: Joey describes peeing with the Rockettes as the bathroom experience.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's dry 'there's my fantasy come true' — playing as if this is exactly the life ambition he's been working toward.
jokes.explanation: A quick follow-up beat that gets a laugh by riding Joey's joke. Chandler's sarcasm is well deployed but this is essentially a reaction joke — it wouldn't exist without joke 17. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?! A twinkie?!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: *gags and covers mouth*

jokes.text: That's all right, I saw a kitchen this morning. On TV.
jokes.setup: The apartment owner offers to show Chandler the kitchen of the amazing apartment.
jokes.punchline: Chandler deflects with absurdist nonchalance — he's already 'seen a kitchen' today... on television. Implying his life is so bachelor-minimal that TV kitchens count.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical joke. 'I saw a kitchen this morning' is already mildly funny — then 'On TV' recontextualizes it as a confession about Chandler's domestic life. Two beats, perfectly timed, highly quotable. Strong character integration: this is exactly how Chandler would deflect from confronting a life upgrade.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: She's not that smart. I mean, she makes a paper towel look intelligent.

jokes.text: Come on, it's my birthday. Let me live vicariously! / Dad, you really don't want to do that.
jokes.setup: Jack pushes for details about Richard's young girlfriend, wanting to live vicariously.
jokes.punchline: Monica's deadpan 'Dad, you really don't want to do that' — because she IS the twinkie, so living vicariously through Richard means living vicariously through his relationship with her.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed dramatic irony joke — the audience knows what Monica knows, and her restraint is funnier than any outburst would be. The line works on two levels simultaneously. Solid rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Geller
dialogue.line: She's very young, very firm... everything's where it's supposed to be.

jokes.text: You got your own little speedster. / Maybe one of these weekends you can borrow the car and I could...
jokes.setup: Jack is teasing Richard about his young girlfriend with car metaphors.
jokes.punchline: Jack begins to suggest Richard could borrow his car so Jack could... the implication being Jack would then pursue Richard's girlfriend. The unfinished sentence is the joke.
jokes.explanation: An interrupted-sentence joke that works because the audience completes it. The setup is a bit labored with the car metaphors, but the pay-off (Jack essentially propositioning Richard's girlfriend) lands. Amplified by the next beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what this is like? It's like being in the Rockettes!

jokes.text: Dad, I beg you not to finish that sentence! / What? I'm kidding! / You know I'd never let him touch the Porsche.
jokes.setup: Monica panics, thinking her dad is about to suggest going after Richard's girlfriend (who is Monica). Jack claims he was joking.
jokes.punchline: Jack's punchline reveals he was only kidding about the girl — but he's entirely serious about the Porsche. The car > the woman reversal.
jokes.explanation: A nice two-level misdirect: Monica misreads the sentence, we think it's resolved, then Jack reveals the Porsche is the actual punchline. Character-specific (Jack's vanity about the car pays off immediately) and structurally clean. Gets an extra boost from the absurd prioritization of a car over human relationships.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could those Rockettes BE any more in our bathroom?

jokes.text: Blond girl? You're in room two. Not-so-blond girl, you're with me.
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe arrive at the tattoo parlor.
jokes.punchline: The tattoo artist's casual categorization of Phoebe as 'not-so-blond girl' is a blunt, slightly insulting way to distinguish between two women.
jokes.explanation: A quick throwaway that gets a mild laugh from the casual rudeness. Functional scene-transition humor without much depth.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I've seen a lot of kitchens. I'm on TV, remember? I see kitchens all the time.

jokes.text: Come on, what is this, 1922? / What's 1922? / Just, you know, a long time ago. / When men used to tell women what to do a lot.
jokes.setup: Rachel invokes 1922 as a symbol of old-fashioned gender oppression to argue Phoebe shouldn't let Ross control her.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe has no idea what 1922 refers to — forcing Rachel to explain the entire concept of historical patriarchy from scratch, which deflates the rhetoric.
jokes.explanation: A neat character joke where Phoebe's obliviousness forces Rachel to backpedal from her own feminist speech. The comedy comes from the rhetorical energy being completely deflated by Phoebe's sincerity. Strong character integration for both.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, check it out! I'm in a kitchen!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not a kitchen, that's a set.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Could it BE any more of a kitchen?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, just... stop talking.

jokes.text: Then there was suffrage, which was a good thing. But it sounds horrible.
jokes.setup: Rachel is trying to explain the history of women's rights to Phoebe.
jokes.punchline: Rachel notes that 'suffrage' — despite being the word for the right to vote — sounds like 'suffering,' and she acknowledges the phonetic horror even while endorsing the concept.
jokes.explanation: A clever wordplay observation that's also character-consistent: Rachel is smart enough to recognize the etymological trap but not so polished that she'd just move past it. The 'but it sounds horrible' acknowledgment is self-aware in a charming way. Well-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Geller
dialogue.line: You know, when I bought that Porsche, I thought I was going through a midlife crisis. Turns out I was just making a down payment on one.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Geller
dialogue.line: Richard's not going through a midlife crisis either. He's just trading in his old model for a newer one.

jokes.text: How you doing? I'm a twinkie! / Really? I'm a hero.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just been told she's the 'twinkie' (Richard's young girlfriend), and runs into Joey.
jokes.punchline: Joey responds that he is a 'hero' — meaning the sandwich — in a perfectly Joey non-sequitur that deflates the drama of Rachel's revelation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. The wordplay (twinkie/hero as both snack foods and slang) is elegant, and Joey's delivery — completely oblivious to Rachel's emotional context, totally absorbed in his sandwich identity — is perfect character comedy. The joke works on a pun level AND a character level simultaneously. 'I'm a hero' as Joey's self-descriptor is inspired. High quotability, exceptional character integration. Approaches the 8-anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Jack Geller
dialogue.line: You know, we could borrow Richard's speedster.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Dad, no!

jokes.text: My parents are dead. / God, you are so lucky!
jokes.setup: Monica suggests they tell Richard's parents first to ease into the revelation. Richard reveals his parents are dead.
jokes.punchline: Monica's immediate 'God, you are so lucky!' — treating dead parents as a tactical advantage in avoiding an awkward conversation.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely dark and surprising joke. The setup (dead parents) is a conversation-stopper, but Monica's reflexive response reframes parental death as enviable — because she dreads her own parents' reaction so much. The speed of 'God, you are so lucky!' is crucial; the lack of hesitation makes it funnier and more revealing of Monica's anxiety. Excellent economy and structure. One of the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Geller
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not saying you can't see Rachel, I'm just saying if you're going to park in my driveway, you need to be very careful.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Mr. Geller, I appreciate that, I really do.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Geller
dialogue.line: My car is very sensitive. One scratch and I'm out $500.

jokes.text: I mean... Well, you know what I mean.
jokes.setup: Monica realizes she just called Richard lucky for having dead parents.
jokes.punchline: Her flustered, inadequate walk-back — 'Well, you know what I mean' — which doesn't help at all. The audience watches her dig the hole slightly deeper.
jokes.explanation: A follow-through beat on joke 27 that functions as a cringe extension. Not as strong on its own — it's just Monica failing to recover — but it milks the previous joke correctly.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My mom was really open-minded. She was always like, 'Phoebe, you can be anything you want to be.'

jokes.text: Judy! Going to the bathroom. Good for you!
jokes.setup: Richard and Monica are trying to sneak out of the party separately. Richard's wife Judy announces she's going to the bathroom at a socially awkward moment.
jokes.punchline: Richard's strained 'Good for you!' — an obviously over-enthusiastic response to a mundane announcement, betraying his nerves.
jokes.explanation: A nice cringe-comedy beat where Richard's cover is almost blown by the most mundane announcement imaginable. The over-correction ('Good for you!') is character-appropriate and gets a laugh from the discomfort.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know, it's like when the Pilgrims came over on the Mayflower and invented Thanksgiving.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, the Native Americans were already here.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know that! I'm not stupid. They were... somewhere else.

jokes.text: I know. He's a new man. It's like a scene from Cocoon.
jokes.setup: Judy says Richard is like a new man with his young girlfriend.
jokes.punchline: Jack compares it to Cocoon — the film about elderly people being rejuvenated — landing perfectly in the parents' cultural frame of reference while being slightly self-incriminating.
jokes.explanation: A generationally specific reference that works because it's so exactly right for Jack's character and age. The joke is in the precision of the choice — not just 'some old movie' but specifically Cocoon, which is about rejuvenation through youth. Solid.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So anyway, that's why they called it the Renaissance.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, that's not even close to what the Renaissance was.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, excuse me for not being a history major. I thought it was called that because people kept saying 'the Renaissance, the Renaissance' and it sounded like 'the re-birth, the re-birth.'

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's... actually not wrong, but not for the reason you think.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: See? I'm basically an art historian now.

jokes.text: So, Jack, ever think about trading me in for a younger model? / Of course not. / With you, it's like I've got two 25-year-olds.
jokes.setup: Judy is fishing for reassurance from Jack that he wouldn't leave her for a younger woman.
jokes.punchline: Jack's reassurance is technically flattering ('two 25-year-olds') but structured as a mathematical trade that somewhat misses the emotional point.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully calibrated joke about how men try to compliment older women and fail sideways. 'Two 25-year-olds' is technically a high valuation but the framing (she's equivalent to two younger women) reveals Jack's transactional worldview. Judy's laugh-and-shrug reaction is the correct beat. Strong character integration for both Gellers.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I want to get a tattoo. Something that really represents me, you know? Something empowering.

dialogue.speaker: Tattoo Artist
dialogue.line: Absolutely. I love it. What are you thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I want it right here on my ankle. Something small but meaningful.

dialogue.speaker: Tattoo Artist
dialogue.line: Perfect. Let me just get this needle ready and we'll put it right on your elbow.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: My elbow?!

dialogue.speaker: Tattoo Artist
dialogue.line: What? That's what you said.

jokes.text: Oh, please. I saw the way you were checking out his moldings.
jokes.setup: Chandler insists he doesn't want the apartment.
jokes.punchline: Joey has noticed Chandler ogling the apartment's architectural details ('moldings') and calls him out in a way that sounds unintentionally provocative.
jokes.explanation: A mild double-entendre that works primarily because 'checking out his moldings' sounds vaguely risqué in a way Joey is entirely oblivious to. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So what are you in the mood for tonight?

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Well, you know me. I'm more of a... sandwich guy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A sandwich? Richard, I'm dessert!

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: I know, but sandwiches are more... substantial. They stick with you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, so I'm just a little treat? Something sweet you have after the real meal?

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: That's not what I meant—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, it's fine. I get it. I'm the dessert. The thing you enjoy but don't really need.

jokes.text: I've already got an apartment that I love. / It wouldn't kill you to say it once in a while.
jokes.setup: Chandler says he loves his apartment and doesn't need another.
jokes.punchline: Joey responds as if the apartment is a partner who deserves verbal affirmation — treating Chandler's lack of verbal apartment-appreciation as a relationship failure.
jokes.explanation: A sharp absurdist pivot that applies relationship logic to real estate. Joey's earnestness makes this land — he genuinely believes apartments deserve to hear they're loved. The joke also sets up the theme of Joey's emotional attachment to their shared space, making it narratively resonant.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We should tell your parents first.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: My parents are dead.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, that's convenient.

jokes.text: I may have to bring in somebody once a week to lick the silverware.
jokes.setup: Joey is defending his ability to live alone and afford a place without a roommate.
jokes.punchline: Joey throws in that he might need to hire someone to lick the silverware — a callback to the cold open's 'you lick and you put' dispute, now reframed as a service Joey would miss.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully executed callback. What started as a disgusting habit Chandler complained about has been transformed by Joey into something he'd pay for — an absurdist reversal that recontextualizes the cold open perfectly. The callback rewards attentive viewers and reveals Joey's character: he genuinely doesn't understand why this is gross. One of the episode's best constructed jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: So, Jack, I was thinking we could, uh, organize your tool shed. Really get those wrenches lined up. Alphabetically? By size? I'm flexible.

dialogue.speaker: Jack Geller
dialogue.line: ...It's just a tool shed.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Right, right. But think about it — the *potential*. We could really make this work. I mean, this could change everything for us.

jokes.text: We're not Bert and Ernie.
jokes.setup: Chandler argues they didn't agree to be roommates forever
jokes.punchline: He invokes Bert and Ernie — Sesame Street's iconic odd-couple roommates — as the alternative to what they are
jokes.explanation: A good pop culture tag on an emotional moment. The Bert and Ernie comparison is apt (odd-couple roommates, one neat, one messy) and adds levity to what could be a genuinely sad scene.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Geller
dialogue.line: It's like Cocoon, except Richard actually came back!

jokes.text: You can spend more quality time with your real friends... the spoons!
jokes.setup: The roommate fight is escalating and Joey wants to get in a final dig at Chandler's germophobia about shared utensils.
jokes.punchline: Joey weaponizes Chandler's earlier disgust at spoon-sharing, sarcastically suggesting the spoons are Chandler's true companions.
jokes.explanation: A solid callback that turns Chandler's fastidiousness into an insult. 'Your real friends... the spoons' is a good line — the ellipsis beat before 'the spoons' lands the reveal well. Serves as a satisfying end to the roommate fight.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Geller
dialogue.line: Are you thinking about trading me in for a younger model?

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Geller
dialogue.line: Don't be ridiculous. Besides, you're not that old. And you've still got a pretty good chassis.

jokes.text: Whose drink can I freshen?
jokes.setup: Joey and Chandler have just had a tense, escalating fight about whether Joey is moving out.
jokes.punchline: A cheerful, oblivious party guest wanders in with the most mundane possible party-service question, perfectly punctuating the emotional blowup.
jokes.explanation: A classic sitcom deflation beat — the emotional moment is punctured by the most mundane possible intrusion. Works well as scene punctuation. The timing is everything here, and it lands because it's exactly the wrong moment for it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not interested in your apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why not? It has a beautiful exposed beam.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A what?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: An exposed beam. The architectural feature.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, stop saying it like that.

jokes.text: Remember that video of Mom and Dad? / Yeah? / Well, I just caught the live show.
jokes.setup: Monica looks shaken. Ross asks if she's okay.
jokes.punchline: Monica reveals she walked in on her parents having sex — described as 'the live show' versus a video Ross presumably already knows about (an earlier episode callback).
jokes.explanation: Tight, precise structure. The setup ('remember that video?') creates dread, then 'I just caught the live show' lands with maximum impact and minimum words. The video reference implies a running gag about the Geller parents being inadvertently sexual exhibitionists, which makes Ross's horrified 'Ew!' the perfect button. Strong episode-level payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know, this apartment... it's like my girlfriend. It needs constant attention, it's always demanding something from me, and if I don't give it what it wants, it shuts me out.

jokes.text: Ew!
jokes.setup: Monica tells Ross she just saw their parents having sex live.
jokes.punchline: Ross's single-syllable 'Ew!' — which says everything and adds nothing while being the exact right response.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy (one syllable), but minimum invention. The laugh comes from the perfectly calibrated single-word reaction. It works, but it's entirely reactive.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can afford to live alone now.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? How?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm just gonna shower once a week. That'll save me a fortune on water.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that's disgusting.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'll just use a lot of cologne.

jokes.text: Your son isn't seeing anyone, is he? / Not that I know of. / I was thinking, why doesn't he give Monica a call?
jokes.setup: Richard is trying to deflect suspicion by acting innocent. He casually suggests setting up Monica with... Ross.
jokes.punchline: Richard suggests Monica and Ross should 'give each other a call' — which is darkly comic given that Ross is their BROTHER and that Richard is already dating Monica.
jokes.explanation: A nicely layered dramatic irony joke — Richard is so desperate to throw Judy off the scent that he suggests Monica date her own brother. The audience knows two things the character doesn't, making the joke richer on rewatch. Good character work for Richard (his flustered improvisation).

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We didn't commit to live together forever.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're not Bert and Ernie.

jokes.text: Mom, there are so many people in my life. Some are seeing people and some aren't. Is that crystal?
jokes.setup: Judy asks Ross if he knew Monica was seeing someone, putting him on the spot.
jokes.punchline: Ross deflects with a comically vague non-answer — 'there are so many people in my life' — and then pivots to admiring the crystal, the most obvious deflection possible.
jokes.explanation: Ross's panic-deflection is well-constructed — the non-answer is so obviously evasive it's funny, and 'Is that crystal?' is the perfect too-obvious subject change. Character-consistent for Ross (terrible at deception).

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You're moving out? Just like that? After everything we've been through?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, we talked about this—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, I get it. You know what? Fine. Just... take your clean spoons with you.

jokes.text: A real doctor? / No, a doctor of meat. / Of course he's a real doctor.
jokes.setup: Monica describes her new boyfriend as 'a doctor.'
jokes.punchline: Monica's sarcastic 'No, a doctor of meat' in response to Judy's redundant clarifying question.
jokes.explanation: A quick, punchy sarcasm beat. 'Doctor of meat' is a good nonsense phrase. Not exceptional but gets a solid laugh and characterizes the Monica-Judy dynamic well.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I found an old video of Mom and Dad from like 20 years ago.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, please tell me you didn't watch it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I had to! And let me tell you, I cannot unsee what I saw.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, what? What did you see?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Let's just say Mom and Dad were very... close on that tape.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh God, oh God, oh God! And I had to LIVE with them while they were doing that!

jokes.text: That's impossible. He's got a twinkie in the city. / I'm the twinkie.
jokes.setup: Jack is told that Monica and Richard are 'an item.' Jack dismisses it because Richard has a young girlfriend.
jokes.punchline: Monica's deadpan 'I'm the twinkie' — the reveal landing on Jack at maximum impact.
jokes.explanation: The episode's structural payoff joke. Three words — 'I'm the twinkie' — deliver maximum information and comedic impact. The structure is impeccable: the term 'twinkie' has been used by the Gellers all episode without knowing it described their daughter, and now Monica gets to own it. The economy is nearly perfect. High quotability. One of the top moments of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, he's a real doctor. He just specializes in the care and treatment of the completely insane.

jokes.text: Upstairs in the bathroom, right before you felt up Mom!
jokes.setup: Jack denies having said Richard was happy. Monica challenges him on when he said it.
jokes.punchline: Monica reveals she overheard this in the bathroom — where she also accidentally witnessed her parents being intimate — the same traumatic 'live show' from earlier.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully timed callback that recontextualizes the earlier trauma. 'Right before you felt up Mom!' — delivered in the middle of a family confrontation — is both a devastating information bomb AND a reminder of Monica's earlier horror. The juxtaposition of this sentence in the middle of a serious reveal argument is what makes it land so hard. Great callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm the Twinkie.

jokes.text: Oh, I love it. / I know, so do I! / Okay, let me see yours. / Let's see yours again. / We just saw mine. Let me see yours.
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe are comparing their tattoos. Rachel has clearly gotten hers; the question is what Phoebe got.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe keeps deflecting — 'let's see yours again' — when it's her turn, building comedic tension before the reveal that she got nothing (or almost nothing).
jokes.explanation: The escalating evasion is a well-used sitcom device. Each deflection ratchets up the anticipation. Works as a setup mechanism for the payoff jokes about Phoebe's non-tattoo.

dialogue.speaker: Jack Geller
dialogue.line: When did I say Richard was happy?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, you didn't say it. I saw it.

jokes.text: I was gonna get it, but he came in with this needle. / And did you know they do this with needles? / Really? You don't say? Because mine was licked on by kittens!
jokes.setup: Phoebe explains she chickened out because of the needle. Rachel is furious — it was Phoebe's idea.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's withering 'Because mine was licked on by kittens!' — pointing out the obvious: all tattoos involve needles, the whole plan was Phoebe's, and now Rachel has one and Phoebe doesn't.
jokes.explanation: A great comedic line. 'Mine was licked on by kittens!' is the right level of absurd specificity — it's not just sarcasm, it's a vividly imagined alternative tattoo application method that makes the absurdity concrete. The escalation from disbelief to withering sarcasm to absurd image is well-paced. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I was going to get a tattoo, but then I found out it was permanent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, that's the whole point of a tattoo.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know that NOW.

jokes.text: Plastic spoons! / Great! / Lick away, my man!
jokes.setup: Joey brings Chandler a peace offering after their fight.
jokes.punchline: It's plastic spoons — a callback to the silverware fight — with Chandler's 'lick away, my man!' completing the reconciliation with a jokey reference to their argument's origin.
jokes.explanation: A warm and well-constructed callback that closes the silverware thread by turning the argument into a reconciliation gesture. The plastic spoons as a gift is a perfect Joey move — thoughtful in his own idiosyncratic way. 'Lick away, my man!' is a good closing line.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Needles are sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh wow, really? Because I thought they were made of jello and awesomeness.

jokes.text: These will go great in my new place till I get real ones.
jokes.setup: Joey takes the plastic spoons warmly, implying he'll use them in his current home.
jokes.punchline: He then mentions 'my new place' — revealing that even the peace-offering moment is tinged with the reality that he really is moving out.
jokes.explanation: An emotional gut-punch disguised as a casual line. The comedy is the contrast between the warmth of the moment and the reminder that Joey actually intends to leave. Works both dramatically and comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I got you some plastic spoons.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Plastic spoons? What am I, camping?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I thought you might like them. You know, for eating ice cream straight from the container.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That is disgusting.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, but you do it anyway. So here, use these.

jokes.text: I can't use these forever. They're no friend of the environment.
jokes.setup: Chandler is confused about Joey leaving; Joey tries to explain with practical reasoning.
jokes.punchline: Joey's environmental concern about plastic spoons — in a conversation about his major life decision to move out — is a characteristic non-sequitur deflection.
jokes.explanation: A nice Joey moment — his sudden pivot to environmental responsibility is funny because it's both sincere and completely beside the point. Character-consistent and slightly absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Are you okay with me leaving?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, of course! I'm not gonna leave you high and dry... I'm gonna leave you high and REALLY dry.

jokes.text: I've never been lower or wetter.
jokes.setup: Joey asks if Chandler is 'cool' with him moving out — doesn't want to leave him 'high and dry.'
jokes.punchline: Chandler's literal inversion of the idiom — 'I've never been lower or wetter' — expressing genuine distress through the mechanics of language play.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Inverting 'high and dry' to 'lower or wetter' is elegant wordplay that simultaneously functions as genuine emotional honesty — Chandler IS emotionally devastated, and the joke lets him express it while maintaining his defensive humor armor. The economy is exceptional. This is the caliber of joke the 8-anchor represents: surprising, quotable, character-perfect, and structurally flawless.

jokes.text: Why do you get to keep the table? / I did pay for half of it. / I paid for the other half.
jokes.setup: Chandler says he'll put the foosball table in Joey's old room.
jokes.punchline: Joey and Chandler both establish their ownership claims — each having paid exactly half — leaving the dispute perfectly unresolvable through logic.
jokes.explanation: A functional setup for the foosball bet. The symmetrical ownership claim is mildly amusing. Works as scene mechanics more than a joke itself.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Your sister's a...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Which sister?

jokes.text: Your men will get scored on more times than your sister.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey agree to play foosball to settle ownership of the table.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's trash talk uses 'scored on' as a double entendre about both foosball and Joey's sister's promiscuity.
jokes.explanation: A good trash-talk joke with a double meaning. 'Scored on' does dual service, and invoking Joey's sister adds a specific Tribbiani family detail. The response ('Whoa, whoa, whoa... which sister?') is the actual payoff — see joke 54.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line:
It's not a dot, it's a...
(long pause)
...it's a period. You know, like at the end of a sentence?

jokes.text: Whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa! / Which sister?
jokes.setup: Chandler insults Joey's sister as trash talk before their foosball game.
jokes.punchline: Joey's reaction is not to defend his sister's honor — it's to clarify WHICH sister Chandler means, implying multiple sisters have reputations that might apply.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. The pause ('Whoa, whoa, whoa') creates expectation of indignation, then 'Which sister?' completely subverts it — Joey isn't offended by the implication, only by the ambiguity. It reveals character (Joey has many sisters, apparently none exempt from Chandler's insult), it's perfectly structured, it's highly quotable, and the beat of the pause before the question is a comedic masterpiece of timing. This is what a 9 looks like: unexpected, character-specific, perfectly economical, and earns its laugh through craft rather than shock alone.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My mother used to say the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Right before she stabbed me.

jokes.text: What? You didn't get one. / Okay. Well then, what is this? / What are we looking at? / That blue freckle? / That's my tattoo.
jokes.setup: The friends discover Phoebe didn't get a tattoo after all. Phoebe reveals what she does have.
jokes.punchline: The 'tattoo' is so small and indistinct that the group can't tell what they're looking at — it's described as a 'blue freckle.'
jokes.explanation: A strong visual gag — the physical comedy of everyone squinting at Phoebe's microscopic tattoo is a classic multi-cam setpiece. 'Blue freckle' is the perfect descriptor. Works well as a physical punchline to the tattoo subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, why is my bra in your apartment?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can explain! I use it as a slingshot!

jokes.text: I got her in the chair, he barely touched her with the needle, she screamed and that was it.
jokes.setup: Rachel explains how Phoebe's 'tattoo' happened.
jokes.punchline: The description reduces Phoebe's dramatic chicken-out to its physical minimum: one touch of the needle, one scream, done.
jokes.explanation: A crisp narrative joke that efficiently conveys the image of Phoebe's aborted tattoo session. Rachel's exasperation is well channeled. Functional and amusing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay, thanks for the help, but uh... you know what? Maybe you should just stick to watching. Your hand-eye coordination isn't exactly legendary.

jokes.text: This is exactly what I wanted. This is a tattoo of the Earth as seen from a great, great distance. It's the way my mother sees me from heaven.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is embarrassed and defensive about her non-tattoo dot.
jokes.punchline: She reframes a blue dot as a spiritually meaningful image: 'the Earth as seen from a great, great distance' — a tortured but earnest post-hoc justification.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. Only Phoebe Buffay would genuinely reframe a blue dot as a cosmic spiritual portrait. The logic is internally consistent with her character's mystical worldview, the image is both funny and oddly touching, and 'as seen from a great, great distance' is perfectly calibrated absurdism. The 'great, great distance' repetition is key — one 'great' wouldn't be funny enough. This is exceptional character comedy that justifies scoring above 8.

jokes.text: Oh, what a load of crap! That is a dot! Your mother's in heaven going, 'Where the hell's my lily, you wuss!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe offers her spiritual reframing of the dot as a tattoo.
jokes.punchline: Monica cuts through it completely, then voices what Phoebe's deceased mother is presumably saying from heaven — in very unspiritual terms.
jokes.explanation: A superb reaction joke that demolishes Phoebe's cosmic reframe with one word ('crap') then extends to a darkly funny callback — Phoebe's dead mother in heaven, demanding the lily she was supposed to get, calling her daughter a 'wuss.' The callback to the original lily plan makes this land with extra force. Monica's straight-talking aggression is perfectly deployed. High quotability and strong craft.

jokes.text: That is not a tattoo! This is a tattoo!
jokes.setup: Monica challenges Phoebe's claim that her dot is a real tattoo.
jokes.punchline: Monica reveals she got a tattoo too — the visual of Monica having secretly gotten one during the same trip is the payoff.
jokes.explanation: A good surprise reveal that recontextualizes Monica's whole participation in the tattoo trip. The structure borrows from 'this is not an X, THIS is an X' — a reliable escalation format — and the visual payoff of Monica actually having a tattoo is satisfying.

jokes.text: You got a tattoo? / Maybe.
jokes.setup: Rachel is shocked that Monica secretly got a tattoo.
jokes.punchline: Monica's coy 'Maybe' — she clearly did, but the deflection is characteristically Monica.
jokes.explanation: A quick beat that functions as a comic button. 'Maybe' after obviously having a tattoo is mildly funny but not notable on its own.

jokes.text: But just a little one. Phoebe got the whole world!
jokes.setup: Monica is qualifying her tattoo revelation.
jokes.punchline: Monica's callback to Phoebe's cosmic framing — 'Phoebe got the whole world' — sarcastically validates Phoebe's ridiculous reframe while rubbing it in.
jokes.explanation: A sharp callback that weaponizes Phoebe's own cosmic logic against her. 'Phoebe got the whole world' accepts the premise sarcastically and escalates it — Phoebe's dot is now mockingly grand. Economical and pointed.

jokes.text: So is it sore? Or can you do stuff?
jokes.setup: Ross is clearly turned on by Rachel's tattoo. He's trying to ask if they can have sex.
jokes.punchline: 'Can you do stuff?' — the most awkward possible euphemism, delivered with sheepish horniness.
jokes.explanation: A strong character comedy beat. 'Can you do stuff?' is a perfectly Ross euphemism — he can't quite say what he means, defaulting to the most nebulous possible phrasing. The audience knows exactly what he means, and that gap between implication and phrasing is funny. Character-specific humor at its best.

jokes.text: I guess. / Save us some pizza.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel's exchange implies they're going to be occupied. Monica and Phoebe realize what's happening.
jokes.punchline: Monica's casual 'Save us some pizza' — she and Phoebe graciously exit while making it perfectly clear they know exactly what Ross and Rachel are about to do.
jokes.explanation: The 'save us some pizza' exit line is economical and knowing. Monica's delivery of something completely mundane — as if the only concern is food — is the joke. Works as a graceful comedic button to the tattoo subplot.

jokes.text: You guys will still come visit me, right? / Oh, yeah! You got the big TV. / We'll be over there all the time. / Except when we are here.
jokes.setup: Joey, getting emotional about leaving, asks if everyone will visit him.
jokes.punchline: The friends immediately confirm they'll visit — because of the big TV, not Joey. Then the qualifier 'except when we are here' underlines the pragmatic rather than sentimental motivation.
jokes.explanation: A warm joke that deflates the sentimentality while also affirming it — the friends will visit, just not for the reasons Joey wants. The 'except when we are here' addition is the best beat, laying bare the transactional honesty. Character-appropriate for this group of friends.

jokes.text: Who's gonna eat all of our food and tie up our phone lines... / Is that my bra?
jokes.setup: Monica begins a sentimental list of things she'll miss about Joey — implying it's building to something genuine.
jokes.punchline: She's interrupted by noticing her bra among Joey's belongings — the sentimental speech derailed by confusion/betrayal.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed misdirect. The setup leads the audience to expect sentimental closure; the punchline is Monica's bra in Joey's box. The interruption is precisely timed and the 'Is that my bra?' reads as both accusatory and baffled. Good structure.

jokes.text: We used it to fling water balloons off the roof. Remember? Those kids couldn't even get theirs across the street.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey explain what they used Monica's bra for.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that a bra was repurposed as a water balloon launcher, and Joey's pride at their superior range versus the neighborhood kids.
jokes.explanation: A great character moment for Joey and Chandler — the bra-as-slingshot is an inspired absurd detail, and Joey's competitive pride ('those kids couldn't even get theirs across the street') is perfect. Tells you everything about their friendship and apartment life in two sentences.

jokes.text: You want me to... give you a hand with the foosball table? / Nah... / You keep it. You need the practice.
jokes.setup: Joey and Chandler are saying goodbye. Chandler offers to help with the foosball table.
jokes.punchline: Joey graciously lets Chandler keep the table he won — then can't resist 'you need the practice,' a final friendly dig.
jokes.explanation: A bittersweet character moment where Joey's generosity and competitive spirit coexist. 'You need the practice' lands because it's simultaneously a dig AND a way to make the moment lighter. Well-executed closing character beat.

jokes.text: When am I gonna see you? / I'm guessing tonight at the coffeehouse.
jokes.setup: Chandler is getting emotional and asks 'when am I gonna see you?' — as if Joey is moving to another country.
jokes.punchline: Joey gently (and correctly) points out that they'll see each other tonight at Central Perk — the reality deflating the drama of the farewell.
jokes.explanation: A warm, economical closing joke that punctures Chandler's drama with Joey's practical clarity. The understatement is perfect — Joey isn't being dismissive, he's just very literal. The joke earns emotional resonance because we understand why Chandler is being dramatic even as we appreciate Joey bringing him back to earth.

tmdb_overview: After having a fight with Chandler, Joey decides to move out. Rachel and Phoebe decide to get tattoos. And, on his birthday, Mr. Geller receives the unsettling news that his best friend and his daughter are dating.
insight: Mid-tier outing buoyed by character comedy, but 54 jokes in 22 minutes yields uneven landing rates.
